newsitem.title: USA: E. coli cases in West mount as probe continues.
newsitem.headline: E. coli cases in West mount as probe continues.

text.p: The number of confirmed or suspected cases of illnesses caused by a strain of E. coli reported in three Western states and Canada's Vancouver area topped 65 as investigators worked on Saturday to isolate the cause of bacterial poisonings that are believed linked to natural apple juice.

In Washington state, where the outbreak was first reported on Wednesday, 17 cases of E. coli poisoning have been confirmed and around 10 additional cases of illness are suspected, according to the Seattle/King Country Department of Public Health.

Food and Drug Administration officials and state health authorities have been working with the trendy California juice company, Odwalla Inc to determine whether its unpasteurized apple juice may be the source, as suspected.
Because the potentially-lethal bacterial disease can take up to 10 days to strike and symptoms can differ greatly, the full extent of the illnesses may not be know for days.

Symptoms of the disease, which affects children most severely, include diarrhoea, sometimes accompanied by bleeding, stomach cramps and a slight fever. More severe cases can result in kidney failure, brain damage and death.

In most of the cases so far identified, a common thread among victims has been recent drinking of apple juice-based natural fruit drinks from Half Moon Bay, Calif.-based Odwalla, which promotes its fresh fruit drinks as healthful.

Odwalla has voluntarily recalled 16 of its 23 fruit-based products, offered customers refunds and said it would pay medical costs of any victims whose infections were a result of having ingested the company's products.
Its distribution region covers seven Western states and British Columbia.
Four of the states -- New Mexico, Oregon, Texas and Nevada -- have not yet reported victims linked to the outbreak.
The E. coli O157:H7 microbe lives within the intestines of cattle and spreads to humans via fecal contamination of food.
Odwalla prides itself on the freshness of its juices, which contain no preservatives and are unpasteurized. The perishable juice are processed, distributed and sold within two weeks.

San Mateo County, California medical authorities reported five cases of children with E. coli this week, the same number typically reported in an entire year. This is in addition to seven confirmed cases in the state linked with apple juice.
Colorado's Department of Public Health has said it has 15 confirmed or suspected cases, including a dozen associated with having consumed Odwalla juice.
At least 14 of the Washington state victims were reported to have consumed Odwalla drinks.
In Canada, the British Columbia Centre for Disease Control said 11 people were reported to have fallen ill during October from the strain of E. coli involved in the juice poisoning.
Epidemiologists had determined that four of those cases, all small children, were linked to the juice and two were not.

The outbreak has raised questions in the media about the safety of unpasteurized fruit juices and the FDA said it had begun discussions with the industry on how to reduce the risk of a similar incident in the future.
Odwalla stock, which shed one-third of its value on Thursday, steadied on Friday, rising $0.875 to close at $13 on the Nasdaq market.
